::: {.lead}
Abuse online is rarely one account acting alone. Review farms, ticket-scalping
rings, fraud crews, and bot networks are *groups* of accounts working together.
The practical problem is telling a coordinated group apart from the ordinary
users who happen to look similar — and an attacker who knows you are looking
will try to look ordinary.
:::

This experiment compares two ways of finding such groups, because each one
catches rings the other misses.

The **first idea** is that coordinated accounts tend to reuse the same things —
a payment card, a device, an IP address — because getting fresh ones for every
account costs money and effort. Link accounts by what they share, and the lazy
rings light up.

The **second idea** is aimed at the attackers who *do* pay that cost. If every
account has its own card, device, and IP, there is nothing to link them by —
except their behaviour. A ring still has to act on the same targets at roughly
the same time to get its job done. Linking accounts by coordinated behaviour —
same action, same target, same time window — catches groups that share no
infrastructure at all. This page calls that signal **behavioural synchrony**.

Neither idea is enough on its own, and the instructive cases are the ones that
break each method: a benign group that *looks* like a reuse ring, and an
ordinary crowd that *looks* coordinated because everyone wanted the same thing
at once. Most of this experiment is about those failure modes.

::: {.callout-important title="What this is, and what it is not"}
The data here is synthetic, and the abusive groups are detectable by
construction. That makes the mechanics of each method easy to see, but it is
**not** evidence that either method would reach these detection rates on real
telemetry. Read it as a demonstration of *how* the methods work and *where*
they fail, not as a benchmark.

The ground-truth group labels only exist because the data is synthetic. In a
real system they would come from review outcomes, chargebacks, takedowns, and
other imperfect, delayed feedback — never the clean labels used here.
:::

## Meet the five groups

The synthetic population is built along two axes: how much accounts **reuse
identifiers**, and how much they **coordinate behaviour**. Every group is placed
to break at least one method.

| Group | Identifier reuse | Behavioural coordination | Why it is here |
|---|---|---|---|
| `legit` | incidental (household IPs/cards; one shared university network) | none | the ordinary-user background neither method should flag |
| `travel_agent` | heavy but benign (one office IP + one card across 25 staff) | none | false-positive trap — looks exactly like a reuse ring |
| `ring_lazy` | heavy (5 cards, 8 devices, 4 IPs, 3 phones across 60 accounts) | tight (~5-min jitter) | the easy case — reuses identifiers *and* coordinates, so most methods should catch it |
| `ring_careful` | none (every identifier unique) | loose (~30-min jitter) | unique identifiers but coordinated timing — built to be invisible to the identifier method |
| `ring_mid` | partial, one type only (12 devices across 40 accounts) | loosest (~1-hr jitter, 70% turnout) | partial reuse and loose timing — built to sit near the limits of both methods |

The numbers in that grid are construction facts, set in `generate_data.py`: the
group sizes, the identifier counts, the campaign jitter (300 / 1800 / 3600
seconds for lazy / careful / mid), and the mid ring's 70% per-wave
participation. They are not results — they are the design, and they are what
makes each cell of the headline result come out the way it does. (*Jitter* is
the small random timing offset a ring adds between its accounts so they do not
all act at the exact same instant — wider jitter looks less coordinated, but is
harder to keep tight.)

The deliberate overlap is the point. Households share IPs and sometimes cards;
120 legit accounts sit behind a single university egress IP; the travel agent's
25 staff share one office IP and one card. That benign reuse is exactly what an
identifier graph has to avoid mistaking for a ring — and exactly why a
clustering step alone is not a detector.

## Headline result

With the cast and the two ideas in hand, the result reads as a payoff rather
than a cold open: which groups each method recovers.

| Group | Identifier graph | Behavioural synchrony |
|---|---:|---:|
| `legit` | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| `travel_agent` | clustered, scored benign | 0.00 |
| `ring_lazy` | 1.00 | 0.97 |
| `ring_careful` | 0.00 | 0.28 |
| `ring_mid` | 0.00 | 0.00 |

Detected share is the fraction of a group's accounts placed in a flagged
cluster, at each method's default settings.

How to read it: for the abusive rings, a *higher* number is better detection.
For the two benign groups — `legit` and `travel_agent` — the target is *zero*;
any detection there would be a false positive. So the ideal column is high on the
rings and zero on the rest.

The two methods are near-complementary by design. The lazy ring is caught by
*both* — it reuses identifiers *and* coordinates. The careful ring, with unique
identifiers, is invisible to the graph and only partly caught by synchrony at
the default one-hour bucket. The mixed ring slips both at default settings. And
the travel agent is the instructive case: the identifier graph *does* cluster it
— correctly; it is a tight cluster — but the scoring step clears it.

::: {.callout-note}
The `travel_agent` cell needs care. "Clustered, scored benign" is two separate
steps: the graph groups the 25 accounts (they really do share infrastructure),
and a later scoring step finds their CAPTCHA rate and registration timing look
ordinary, so they are not flagged. The coverage figure on the Method 1 page
shows only the *clustering* step, so the travel agent appears there as a full
Method 1 bar. That bar means "grouped," not "flagged" — the distinction is the
whole point of separating clustering from scoring.
:::

The result worth dwelling on is `ring_mid` — though the sweeps narrow what can
honestly be said about it. At each method's *default* settings it is the
adversary both catch least (zero on each), and it is also the most realistic:
partial reuse of one identifier type, loose timing. That much is real. But
loosening Method 1's edge-weight floor from 0.8 to 0.4 recovers about 40% of it,
and dropping Method 2's Jaccard floor to 0.10 recovers nearly all of it — both
with no measured cost to the benign groups. The catch is that *this* population
cannot show a cost: its one large benign reuse group is removed by pruning, its
households are below the cluster-size floor, and its ordinary accounts generate
almost no coincidental synchrony, so the false-positive side of every tradeoff is
structurally absent. The honest claim is therefore narrow — `ring_mid` slips both
at conservative defaults, is partly recoverable by loosening thresholds, and this
dataset cannot say what that loosening would cost on real traffic. Building
benign groups that actually exercise that cost is the clearest next limitation to
close.

The detection shares above are reproduced from the experiment run and
corroborated by the rendered coverage and sweep figures.
